title: TOM-SWE: User Mental Modeling For Software Engineering Agents
one_liner: Pair a coding agent with a second smaller agent that tracks the user's goals, constraints, and preferences so the main agent stays aligned across ambiguous and stateful tasks.
lead: A coding agent can read files, run tests, and edit code, yet still miss what the user actually wants. The failure often appears when instructions are incomplete, preferences were stated earlier, or the task depends on ongoing project context. This paper adds a dedicated user-modeling partner to the coding agent. The partner keeps a lightweight picture of the user's intent and feeds guidance back to the main agent so that task decisions stay aligned across turns.

problem.h2: Why coding agents lose the user's intent
paras: Software tasks are often underspecified. A user may say to fix a bug, but the real goal can include preserving a particular interface, avoiding risky refactors, or matching the style of the rest of the codebase. A strong coding agent can still miss those constraints because they are spread across earlier conversation turns or implied by past choices.

The problem becomes worse in stateful work. As the interaction continues over hours or days, the agent must remember what the user prefers, what tradeoffs were rejected, and what project conventions matter. If all of that is left inside one overloaded agent context, user modeling competes with code reasoning for limited working space.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Split the job into a main coding agent and a small partner that maintains a running model of the user's goals and preferences, then feed that model back into planning and action selection.

paras: The paper changes how a coding agent represents the user. Instead of treating the conversation only as extra prompt text, it maintains an explicit model of the user's current goals, constraints, and preferences.
object.object: The internal representation of user intent in a coding workflow

hidden.name: User intent state
paras: The important hidden quantity is not the text of the latest instruction but the user's actual working intent. That state includes what outcome the user wants, which constraints they care about, and which tradeoffs they are likely to reject. A single message rarely contains all of that.

The paper estimates this hidden state from conversation history and earlier corrections. The second agent maintains it explicitly so that the main coding agent does not need to re-derive the user's preferences from scratch every time it chooses a plan.

heat.caption: High values mark conversation details that strongly affect the correct patch choice.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is what the user is really optimizing for, not just the words in the latest turn.
A dedicated theory-of-mind partner estimates user goals, constraints, and preferences from interaction history, then supplies that state to the main software agent as decision support.

paras: Separating user modeling from code execution helps because the two jobs require different working habits. The coding agent must inspect files, tests, and commands, while the user-modeling partner must track intent across turns. When one component specializes in the second job, important user constraints are less likely to disappear during intense code work.

Persistent user state also helps because many software tasks are sequential. A user's earlier correction should shape later planning even if the current turn does not repeat it. The partner preserves that memory and presents it in a small actionable form so that the main agent can choose a plan that fits both the repository and the user's working style.

math.words: Score each candidate coding action by combining task progress with how well the action matches the maintained user intent state.
math.equation: action_score = task_progress + alpha * intent_match - beta * constraint_violation
symbols: value of one candidate coding action
how much the action moves the software task forward
how well the action fits the stored user goals and preferences
how much the action conflicts with user limits such as scope or interface stability

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Action A fixes the bug by changing a public interface the user wanted to keep stable: task_progress = 0.9, intent_match = 0.2, constraint_violation = 0.8.
Action B fixes the bug with a narrower patch that preserves the interface: task_progress = 0.8, intent_match = 0.9, constraint_violation = 0.1.
The system prefers B because it balances technical progress with the user's stated constraints.

math.note: The paper uses a fuller dual-agent setup than this toy score, but the score captures the main idea: good technical work must also match the user's intent state.

charts.title: Single coding agent
charts.note: The baseline loses intent when tasks are underspecified or depend on earlier turns.

charts.title: ToM-SWE
charts.note: The dual-agent design helps because explicit user modeling keeps constraints and preferences active across the full workflow.

items.html: If the partner over-interprets a vague message, later actions may become misaligned because the stored preference state is wrong.

items.b: Old preferences can overpower new ones.
items.html: Persistent memory can become stale if recent corrections are not weighted strongly enough.
Two agents can disagree or slow the workflow if the handoff between user modeling and action planning is not kept concise.
Update the user state aggressively after corrections, keep the summary compact, and expose uncertainty so that the main agent knows when to ask for clarification.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a coding-task benchmark with ambiguous requests and multi-turn revisions. Compare a standard coding agent against a two-part system where a small partner stores user goals, forbidden actions, and style preferences. Measure task completion, how often the final patch violates user constraints, and how often the agent must ask for clarification.

The demo should prove that explicit user modeling improves alignment because earlier constraints continue to influence later edits, especially on stateful tasks where the latest instruction alone is not enough.
demo.metric_eq: constraint_violation_rate = violating_runs / total_runs ; alignment_gain = dual_agent_success - baseline_success
demo.closing: A strong demo shows fewer constraint violations and higher completion on ambiguous tasks because the system remembers what the user meant across the whole session.
